title: Weather and Aftermath
premise: Felix Underhill, a celebrated restaurant critic who lost his sense of taste after his mother's stroke, returns to the family house for her funeral and finds a stranger named Ada Voss standing among the mourners, greeting relatives by the surname 'Wrenfield' — a name that appears nowhere in Felix's childhood but everywhere in his mother's sealed letters. As Felix and his sister Margot inventory the house's unsaid things — a locked garden room, a second set of photographs, a deed signed by a man who never existed — they discover their mother lived an entire prior life under another name, one she traded away to buy respectability and silence. Ada is the daughter of the family their mother erased, and she has come not for money but for memory: the letters that prove her father loved them both. In the final chapters, as their mother's last lucid recordings degrade into static, Felix must choose between publishing the truth that will restore his career and burying it to protect the inheritance; he forgives Ada, gives her the photographs, and tastes something again at last.
about_author: Isandro Eastwick is the pen name of a former obituary writer from the coastal towns of southern England who spent a decade cataloguing what families refuse to say aloud. 'Weather and Aftermath' is their first novel, written in the intervals between tides.

chapters.title: The Inventory
chapters.summary: Felix, POV, drafts a review he cannot taste, describing food entirely from memory and technique while keeping a private ledger of sentences he has never said to his dying mother. The emotional beat is hollow competence — a man fluent in everything except feeling.

chapters.title: Weather Report
chapters.summary: Margot, POV, calls Felix with news of their mother's death and asks him to come home to Saltmere. She confesses she hasn't entered the garden room since the stroke. The beat is dread disguised as logistics.

chapters.title: A Name Nobody Uses
chapters.summary: The funeral. Felix, POV, watches a grey-coated stranger comfort his aunt using the surname Wrenfield, and no one corrects her. He follows her out into the churchyard rain. The beat is vertigo — the ground of family history shifting.

chapters.title: Ada
chapters.summary: Ada Voss, POV, explains only that she knew their mother 'before,' and leaves a photograph on the porch step: two young women, one unmistakably their mother, laughing in front of a house that isn't theirs. The beat is quiet provocation.

chapters.title: The Garden Room
chapters.summary: Felix and Margot, alternating POV, break the padlock on the garden room and find it preserved like a museum: pre-1970s furniture, a woman's clothing, boxes of letters addressed to E. Wrenfield. The beat is trespass and awe.

chapters.title: Letters to E.
chapters.summary: Felix, POV, reads the first letters — love letters from a Thomas Voss, written during a war or near-war era he can't place against his mother's official biography. Margot refuses to read any. The beat is seduction by the past.

chapters.title: What the Critic Cannot Taste
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, Felix's POV, reconstructing the day his taste vanished — the same week his mother's stroke — and the doctor's verdict: psychogenic. The beat is grief he has been misdiagnosing as medical.

chapters.title: The Deed
chapters.summary: Margot, POV, discovers the house itself was transferred under the Wrenfield name before being re-registered, meaning their entire inheritance rests on a legal fiction. The beat is betrayal arriving through paperwork.

chapters.title: Confrontation at the Sea Wall
chapters.summary: Felix confronts Ada on the shingle beach; she reveals Thomas Voss was her grandfather, and that their mother took his name, his money, and then erased him from every record. The beat is anger meeting its mirror.

chapters.title: Recordings
chapters.summary: Felix, POV, plays his mother's dictaphone tapes made after the stroke — lucid, evasive, half-confessional — and hears her begin a sentence about 'the girl I owed' that dissolves into static. The beat is desperate listening.

chapters.title: Margot's Bargain
chapters.summary: Margot, POV, secretly offers Ada money to leave, believing the family can survive only if the past stays buried; Ada declines but doesn't expose her. The beat is shame and the corruption inheritance breeds.

chapters.title: The Second House
chapters.summary: Felix and Ada travel together to the house in the old photograph, now derelict, where Thomas Voss raised both families unknowingly adjacent. The beat is pilgrimage; the past becomes geography.

chapters.title: Thomas
chapters.summary: Ada, POV, tells the full story of her grandfather — his generosity, his ruin, and how Felix's mother testified against him to secure her own escape. The beat is sympathy turning complicated.

chapters.title: The Offer
chapters.summary: A literary editor, having heard rumors, offers Felix a career-defining book: the true story of the Underhill/Wrenfield deception. Felix, POV, feels ambition wake in him like an appetite. The beat is temptation with a byline.

chapters.title: Static
chapters.summary: Felix, POV, returns to the tapes and realizes they are degrading beyond recovery; whatever full confession his mother recorded is being erased in real time. The beat is panic — memory dying faster than understanding.

chapters.title: Sister Weather
chapters.summary: Margot and Felix fight over whether to publish; she accuses him of doing to their mother in death what she did to Thomas in life. The beat is the family's cruelty becoming visible and inherited.

chapters.title: The Last Lucid Hour
chapters.summary: Among the final tapes, Felix finds one coherent passage: his mother names Ada's father, admits the theft, and asks — explicitly — that the photographs be returned, not the money. The beat is devastating clarity.

chapters.title: Forgiving the Stranger
chapters.summary: Felix, POV, sits with Ada among the old photographs and forgives her — not for intruding, but for being the proof of everything he wanted not to know. The beat is grace arriving without absolution being earned neatly.

chapters.title: Publication
chapters.summary: Felix writes the piece — not the exposé the editor wanted, but an essay about a woman who bought a new name and paid for it with her children's history. The beat is authorship as penance rather than power.

chapters.title: Aftermath
chapters.summary: The essay publishes; the family fractures publicly, the estate enters dispute, and Margot stops speaking to Felix. Ada receives the photographs and the letters. The beat is consequence without consolation.

chapters.title: Taste
chapters.summary: Felix, POV, eats alone at a small restaurant and, mid-meal, taste returns — ordinary, imperfect, overwhelming. He weeps into his plate over something as small as salt. The beat is recovery as loss finally metabolized.

chapters.title: Weather and Aftermath
chapters.summary: Months later, Felix and Margot meet awkwardly at the sold house; Ada sends a letter containing one new photograph — all three mothers, young, unafraid. Felix begins saying the unsaid things aloud. The beat is reconciliation, partial and weathered, but real.
